sections.heading: Key points
sections.content:
*   Research shows a link between chronic pain and issues like anxiety, anger, and depression. 
*   Many common emotional problems are bidirectionally related to chronic pain.
*   Functional limitations caused by chronic pain can result in emotional distress. 

We tend to view [chronic pain](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/chronic-pain "Psychology Today looks at chronic pain") (CP) as a body issue; a problem that lives mainly within our physical system and causes tangible aches, pain, stiffness, tightness, soreness, and general discomfort. But there is an emotional component to chronic pain that is often either overlooked or misunderstood. Understanding the intersection of physical pain and emotional pain is necessary in taking a holistic view of the body-mind dyad.

sections.heading: The Research
sections.content:
This correlation between physical pain and emotional distress continues to be of great interest, and recent research indicates that around 40 percent of individuals with chronic pain experience clinically significant symptoms of [depression](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/depression "Psychology Today looks at depression") or [anxiety](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/anxiety "Psychology Today looks at anxiety") and that “the co-occurrence of chronic pain with depression and anxiety is a significant public health concern” (Aaron et al., 2025).

Meta-analyzed data from 110 studies revealed that among individuals who experienced CP, a range of psychological problems were observed, including depression, anxiety, somatization, [anger](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/anger "Psychology Today looks at anger"), low [self-esteem](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/self-esteem "Psychology Today looks at self-esteem"), and disturbance to normal emotional functioning (Burke et al., 2015).

A 2025 umbrella review concluded that CP and mental disorders frequently co-occur and reported evidence of bidirectional relationships, particularly between depression and chronic pain (Stubbs et al., 2025). This undeniable relationship between the physical and the emotional can help us better understand why and how CP can directly affect emotional functioning.

sections.heading: Depression: “My Body Is Betraying Me”
sections.content:
Clinically speaking, depression is often associated with feelings of hopelessness and helplessness, and for individuals with CP, this sense of helplessness is driven by the feeling that their physical body is failing or betraying them.

CP might be considered a “[stress](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/stress "Psychology Today looks at stress") state,” wherein a person is in a constant state of discomfort. After a prolonged period, a stress state inevitably leads to exhaustion, fatigue, and hypoactivity (low mood).

CP is defined as a recurrent or persistent pain that lasts longer than three months (Raffaeli et al., 2021). For some people, CP lasts far longer than three months and can persist for decades. Existing in this constant stress state has significant neurobiological consequences that invite depression, including changes in brain chemistry, overactivation of the brain’s stress-response system, and the shrinking of key brain areas (Tafet & Nemeroff, 2015).

The prolonged fatigue and negative feelings of body betrayal that come with CP can result in depression and lead to maladaptive responses such as social withdrawal, inability to access adaptive coping mechanisms, and continued low mood (Boyes, 2013).

sections.heading: Anxiety: “What if I Never Get Better?”
sections.content:
CP and anxiety share a complex, bidirectional relationship: Persistent physical pain causes [fear](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/fear "Psychology Today looks at fear") and stress and, at the same time, constant anxiety and fear can cause inflammation, resulting in a vicious cycle (McAllister, 2010).

The fear associated with CP often takes the form of [catastrophic thinking](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/catastrophizing "Psychology Today looks at catastrophic thinking"), such as “What if this gets worse? What if I never feel better? What if this indicates a much larger problem?” Studies find that among people with CP, anxiety responses such as rumination, fixation, avoidance, and cognitive fusion (interpreting thoughts as literal facts) are common (Tenti et al., 2026). The “what ifs” of CP-related anxiety can cause distress: Rumination and fixation cause us to struggle to pay [attention](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/attention "Psychology Today looks at attention") to anything other than our physical pain; avoidance can cause us to neglect care and pain [management](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/leadership "Psychology Today looks at management"); and cognitive fusion can cause us to misinterpret our thoughts and overestimate negative outcomes.

sections.heading: Anger: “I Hate Feeling This Way”
sections.content:
Similar to anxiety, anger is bidirectionally related to CP: Pain can trigger frustration while frustration and anger can worsen inflammation. As with depression and anxiety, anger is commonly observed as having a close relationship with CP.

According to the Mayo Clinic, many people with CP “report feeling angry at themselves or at others on a consistent basis” (Mayo Clinic, 2024). A staggering 70 percent of people with CP report feeling angry at themselves or at their healthcare providers (Black, 2020). Furthermore, some individuals with CP feel a sense of injustice or unfairness, a sense of “why me?” regarding their pain.

While expressions of anger can be coping mechanisms for living with pain, pain management doctor Germaine Rowe points out that it can be counterproductive, as it “puts the body in a state of stress,” causing “a chain of events that end up worsening the pain” (Black, 2020).

To bring it all together and appropriately understand this important connection between CP and emotional functioning, we must accept that CP often causes individuals to feel detached from themselves or from the way they are accustomed to functioning. These functional limitations directly cause emotional dysfunction in the form of depression, anxiety, and anger.

Accepting the viewpoint that there is an undeniable relationship between the physical and the emotional can help us better understand why and how CP affects an individual’s emotional life and recognize that these two parts of our existence are not mutually exclusive.

# Why Chronic Pain Causes Emotional Pain

## Chronic pain extends beyond the physical body and affects the emotions.

### Key points

*   Research shows a link between chronic pain and issues like anxiety, anger, and depression. 
*   Many common emotional problems are bidirectionally related to chronic pain.
*   Functional limitations caused by chronic pain can result in emotional distress. 

We tend to view [chronic pain](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/chronic-pain "Psychology Today looks at chronic pain") (CP) as a body issue; a problem that lives mainly within our physical system and causes tangible aches, pain, stiffness, tightness, soreness, and general discomfort. But there is an emotional component to chronic pain that is often either overlooked or misunderstood. Understanding the intersection of physical pain and emotional pain is necessary in taking a holistic view of the body-mind dyad.

## The Research

This correlation between physical pain and emotional distress continues to be of great interest, and recent research indicates that around 40 percent of individuals with chronic pain experience clinically significant symptoms of [depression](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/depression "Psychology Today looks at depression") or [anxiety](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/anxiety "Psychology Today looks at anxiety") and that “the co-occurrence of chronic pain with depression and anxiety is a significant public health concern” (Aaron et al., 2025).

Meta-analyzed data from 110 studies revealed that among individuals who experienced CP, a range of psychological problems were observed, including depression, anxiety, somatization, [anger](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/anger "Psychology Today looks at anger"), low [self-esteem](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/self-esteem "Psychology Today looks at self-esteem"), and disturbance to normal emotional functioning (Burke et al., 2015).

A 2025 umbrella review concluded that CP and mental disorders frequently co-occur and reported evidence of bidirectional relationships, particularly between depression and chronic pain (Stubbs et al., 2025). This undeniable relationship between the physical and the emotional can help us better understand why and how CP can directly affect emotional functioning.

## Depression: “My Body Is Betraying Me”

Clinically speaking, depression is often associated with feelings of hopelessness and helplessness, and for individuals with CP, this sense of helplessness is driven by the feeling that their physical body is failing or betraying them.

CP might be considered a “[stress](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/stress "Psychology Today looks at stress") state,” wherein a person is in a constant state of discomfort. After a prolonged period, a stress state inevitably leads to exhaustion, fatigue, and hypoactivity (low mood).

CP is defined as a recurrent or persistent pain that lasts longer than three months (Raffaeli et al., 2021). For some people, CP lasts far longer than three months and can persist for decades. Existing in this constant stress state has significant neurobiological consequences that invite depression, including changes in brain chemistry, overactivation of the brain’s stress-response system, and the shrinking of key brain areas (Tafet & Nemeroff, 2015).

The prolonged fatigue and negative feelings of body betrayal that come with CP can result in depression and lead to maladaptive responses such as social withdrawal, inability to access adaptive coping mechanisms, and continued low mood (Boyes, 2013).

## Anxiety: “What if I Never Get Better?”

CP and anxiety share a complex, bidirectional relationship: Persistent physical pain causes [fear](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/fear "Psychology Today looks at fear") and stress and, at the same time, constant anxiety and fear can cause inflammation, resulting in a vicious cycle (McAllister, 2010).

The fear associated with CP often takes the form of [catastrophic thinking](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/catastrophizing "Psychology Today looks at catastrophic thinking"), such as “What if this gets worse? What if I never feel better? What if this indicates a much larger problem?” Studies find that among people with CP, anxiety responses such as rumination, fixation, avoidance, and cognitive fusion (interpreting thoughts as literal facts) are common (Tenti et al., 2026). The “what ifs” of CP-related anxiety can cause distress: Rumination and fixation cause us to struggle to pay [attention](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/attention "Psychology Today looks at attention") to anything other than our physical pain; avoidance can cause us to neglect care and pain [management](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/leadership "Psychology Today looks at management"); and cognitive fusion can cause us to misinterpret our thoughts and overestimate negative outcomes.

## Anger: “I Hate Feeling This Way”

Similar to anxiety, anger is bidirectionally related to CP: Pain can trigger frustration while frustration and anger can worsen inflammation. As with depression and anxiety, anger is commonly observed as having a close relationship with CP.

According to the Mayo Clinic, many people with CP “report feeling angry at themselves or at others on a consistent basis” (Mayo Clinic, 2024). A staggering 70 percent of people with CP report feeling angry at themselves or at their healthcare providers (Black, 2020). Furthermore, some individuals with CP feel a sense of injustice or unfairness, a sense of “why me?” regarding their pain.

While expressions of anger can be coping mechanisms for living with pain, pain management doctor Germaine Rowe points out that it can be counterproductive, as it “puts the body in a state of stress,” causing “a chain of events that end up worsening the pain” (Black, 2020).

To bring it all together and appropriately understand this important connection between CP and emotional functioning, we must accept that CP often causes individuals to feel detached from themselves or from the way they are accustomed to functioning. These functional limitations directly cause emotional dysfunction in the form of depression, anxiety, and anger.

Accepting the viewpoint that there is an undeniable relationship between the physical and the emotional can help us better understand why and how CP affects an individual’s emotional life and recognize that these two parts of our existence are not mutually exclusive.
